items.text: SEASON 5 · EPISODE 10 · DRAFT · SEASON FINALE  Countdown · Wes, Maya, Nadia and Tess · Level L4 · Intermediate support  Commencement. Two thousand in the arena, nine thousand on the stream, live captions, a Spanish channel, a TV station taking the feed through the hub — and Nadia’s last event. Wes runs the stream. Maya stays at the back.  ⚑ RV-136: stream figures illustrative. RV-137: interpreters and captioners as professionals. Some choices run on a clock.

items.title: Commencement
items.stakes: Two thousand in the arena, nine thousand on the stream, a second language, live captions, a TV station taking the feed — and Nadia's last event. Wes runs it. Maya watches.
items.reward: Every graduate heard, captioned and interpreted. Wes answering for his own desk. Maya's hands in her pockets.

objectives.text: Look closer: two things about the day

items.rumor: The question isn't whether Maya can handle it. It's whether she needs to.

items.alt: The arena at 8:30, empty seats, banners hung. Nadia, Wes in his headset, and Maya on the floor in front of the stage.

bubbles.text: Eleven years of these. This is the first one I get to watch.

lines.text: Eleven years of these. This is the first one I get to watch.

items.alt: The plan on one screen: a 100 Mb/s uplink carrying main 8, captions and Spanish 1, and backup 8 Mb/s — 17% used; the station's take via the hub with a direct path ready; captions, Spanish and three-source campus time all ticked.
items.caption: Seventeen percent of the link. Everything written down. Nothing in anyone's head.

items.prompt: Are you sure you don't want to run it? It's Nadia's last one. If I—

options.label: “It's yours. I'll be at the back. Here's who to call for what — and you don't need me for any of it.”
options.reply: …Okay. Then stay at the back. Even if I look at you.

options.label: “Maybe I should, just to be safe.”
“What would you need from me if something broke?”
options.reply: The run-of-show and Tess's number. I've got both.

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #51 · AVERY'S LENS  Give people the feed their job needs  The right signal for a professional is the one that lets them do their work — not the one that was easiest to patch.  The interpreter was given the arena mix: speeches and two thousand families. She needed the reader's microphone, clean.

items.prompt: 8:40. Wes: “Are you sure you don't want to run it? It's Nadia's last one.” What do you do?
items.risk: A system that only works with you in the chair.
timeout: You hesitate. Wes waits, then sits down anyway.
He needed you to say it.

hints.text: What would let everyone respond without you?

options.label: Take the desk — it's too important to learn on
options.result: Wes carries cables all morning. Next year he still hasn't run one.
options.consequence: Safe today, fragile every day after.
options.fail: If only you can run it, the system depends on you.

options.label: “It's yours. I'll be at the back. Here's who to call for what — and you don't need me for any of it.”
options.result: Wes breathes out. “Then stay at the back. Even if I look at you.”
options.consequence: Everything he needs is written down; the job is to let him use it.

options.label: Sit beside him on a second desk ‘just in case’
options.result: He checks your face before every cut.
options.consequence: Hovering is taking the desk slowly.

options.label: Ask Nadia to run it — it's her last one
options.result: Nadia: “I'd like to watch this one. That's the point.”

items.alt: The arena, full. In the interpreter's booth at the side, the Spanish interpreter strains to hear; a callout shows what she hears — fragments of the reader's words under cheering. Her booth feed is the arena PA mix.

bubbles.text: I can't hear the names. I hear two thousand families.

lines.text: Row ten, by the exit, all year. Today she's in the graduates' seats — front row. Her choice.

items.title: She's hearing the room.
items.body: The interpreter's headphones carry the arena PA mix — the same sound the families hear, cheering and all. Speeches were fine. The names, read quickly into a roar, aren't. She needs a clean feed of the reader's microphone — and the rehearsal was in an empty arena.
items.label: Test: what's wrong with her feed — and what does she need?

items.prompt: 9:55. The names start at 10:30. How does Wes fix the interpreter's feed?
known: ◉ Reader mic on its own channel
items.risk: Families hearing the wrong name — or none.
timeout: The fix was one route away.

hints.text: What does her job need to hear?

options.label: Route a clean feed of the reader's microphone to her headphones — and check her voice goes only to the Spanish channel
options.result: The interpreter, at 10:02: “Perfect. I can hear every syllable.”

options.label: Ask her to do her best with the names
options.result: She guesses at forty names. Two families hear the wrong one.
options.consequence: Makes her pay for our patch.

options.label: Skip interpretation during the names
options.result: Spanish-speaking families hear nothing for an hour.
options.consequence: Drops the people the channel is for.
options.fail: Interpretation is for the whole ceremony.

items.label: **Fix it:** give the interpreter the names — and the stream its second language.

items.title: Words at the bottom of the screen
items.body: On 16 March 1980, the first television programs with closed captions were broadcast in the United States, for viewers with a decoder box. Captions later moved into every television and then onto every stream. Each step meant the same thing at a commencement: the name you came to hear, readable by everyone.

items.alt: The names. On the big screen's caption bar: MIRA H., BACHELOR OF SCIENCE, BIOLOGY. Farah watches from the side, smiling.

bubbles.text: Captioned, interpreted — and she heard her own name through the loop.

items.caption: Captioned. Interpreted. Heard.

items.title: The hub, again.
items.body: 10:41: the hub's clock fails again — its second antenna is still on order. Campus time doesn't notice: three sources vote and the hub has no say (One Clock). But the TV station's take passes through the hub's gateway, which follows the hub's clock. On the station's air, the names begin to tear.
items.label: Test: why is campus fine — and why isn't the station?

items.alt: Master control at the hub: a red SYNC alarm on the monitor wall. Tess on the phone.

bubbles.text: Wes? Your feed's tearing on our air. Middle of the names. Is it you?

items.title: ‘If the hub tears’
items.body: Page 6 of Wes's run-of-show, written in April after One Clock: *If the station's take tears and our viewer monitor is clean → check campus time → ask Tess → offer the direct path (agreed with Tess, tested 3 May).* Maya didn't write it. She reviewed it, and changed one word.

items.prompt: 10:42. Tess is on Wes's line. Maya is at the back. What happens?
unknown: Whether Wes will look at you
items.risk: The station's viewers losing the names — and Wes losing the day.
timeout: Wes looks at you. You look back.
He does it himself. You didn't have to decide — but you didn't say it either.

hints.text: What did you build him for?

options.label: Maya walks down and takes the desk
options.result: Wes steps back without a word. You fix nothing he wasn't about to fix.
options.consequence: The day he needed not to need you.
options.fail: Did what you built let him respond without you?

options.label: Wes checks the viewer monitor and campus time, asks Tess what the hub shows, then offers the direct path from page 6. Maya stays where she is.
options.result: Wes: “We're clean at our viewer, campus time's on three sources — it's your gateway. Direct path's up, want it?” Tess switches at 10:45.
options.consequence: Evidence, then the pre-agreed alternative — his, start to finish.

options.label: Restart the campus encoder
options.result: Nine thousand viewers drop in the middle of the names.
options.consequence: Never restart a clean live stream to fix someone else's path.

options.label: Switch campus to hub time so everything ‘matches’
options.result: Every campus clock starts drifting with the hub.

items.alt: At the stream desk, Wes on the phone beside a monitor reading VIEWER CLEAN, captions and Spanish on, campus time three sources. Far behind him, at the back, Maya with her hands in her pockets.

bubbles.text: We're clean at our viewer, campus time's on three sources — it's your gateway. Direct path's up. Want it?

items.alt: System View after 10:45: program, captions and Spanish into the campus encoder; the stream to about 9,000 viewers; the station taking the direct path; the hub gateway unused.
items.caption: Every name, captioned and interpreted, on the stream and on the station's air.

items.alt: The empty arena after the ceremony: confetti on the floor. Nadia, Wes and Maya.

bubbles.text: Eleven years, and I got to watch the last one.

items.title: Left on Maya's keyboard
items.body: After the recessional, Nadia's staff badge is on Maya's keyboard with a note: *Not yours to keep — hand it to facilities Monday. The wiki's got the rest. Go home at five. — N.*

items.alt: The dark arena later that afternoon. Maya alone on the floor, answering her phone: PRIYA, LINDEN ROW DESIGN.

bubbles.text: I've joined a design firm. We draw the systems people like you spend years fixing — a hospital wing, a courthouse, a theater. I need someone who knows what drawings get wrong. Want to draw it right the first time?

items.caption: End of Season 5. Next: *The Drawing Set.*

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  Give every professional the feed their job needs, keep every language on its own channel, leave room on the link — and write the run-of-show so the person on the desk can answer without you. Then stay at the back.
REFLECTION (optional)  · Maya never touched the desk. What would you need to have built, written and practised to be able to stay at the back?
